speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, the Evidence Act requires the Courts to presume the genuineness of laws and reports of judicial decisions contained in books, where such evidence is tendered in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: However, as the presumption only applies to those contained in books, it does not apply to laws or reports published online, even if they are published on official websites authorised by the government of a country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendment will also make clear that the presumption is applicable only to official or authoritative reports of decisions of the courts of a country.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clauses 7 and 43 of the Bill contain three main sets of amendments to the Family Justice Act and the Supreme Court of Judicature Act respectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: These amendments seek to: (a) align the right of appeal between family cases and non-family cases; (b) clarify that all family proceedings must be commenced at the Family Court; and (c) introduce immunity provisions for certain groups of individuals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, under the Family Justice Act, family proceedings can be heard, at first instance, by: (a) the Family Division of the High Court, in which case, appeals are heard by the Court of Appeal; or (b) the Family Courts, in which case, appeals are heard by the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that the right of appeal is consistent across the lower Courts, namely, the Family Court, District Court and Magistrate's Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also amends the Supreme Court of Judicature Act to restrict the right of appeal from the Family Division of the High Court to the Court of Appeal, such that certain interlocutory orders made by the Family Division of the High Court are either not appealable, or appealable only with leave of that Court or the Court of Appeal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This aligns the appeal regime in the Family Division of the High Court, with that applicable to non-family proceedings in the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now touch on the amendments requiring family proceedings to be commenced in the Family Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, the practice is for applications for all family proceedings to be filed in the Family Court, except those proceedings which the Chief Justice has directed to be heard and determined by the Family Division of the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, this exception applies to probate cases involving estates which exceed $5 million in value.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: For family proceedings commenced in the Family Court, the current practice has been to transfer contested matters where the assets are above $5 million or, where the case is complex, to the Family Division of the High Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This practice will continue, subject to any adjustments that may be made by the Chief Justice from time to time.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lastly, the Bill amends the Family Justice Act and the Supreme Court of Judicature Act to confer certain individuals with protection from personal liability where the acts are done in good faith and do not involve any fraud or wilful misconduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Child representatives, appointed to represent the interests of a child, will be protected from personal liability under the Family Justice Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Registered medical practitioners, psychologists, counsellors, social workers or mental health professionals appointed by a Family Court or the High Court to examine or assess a child or person will be protected from personal liability under the Family Justice Act and Supreme Court of Judicature Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The immunity provisions ensure that these professionals, who do not represent any of the parties before the Court and lend their expertise to assist the Court in arriving at a fair and just decision, will be able to perform their duties without fear of legal liability, so long as they act in good faith and without fraud or wilful misconduct.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill also introduces amendments to the Maintenance Orders (Reciprocal Enforcement) Act, Reciprocal Enforcement of Commonwealth Judgments Act and Reciprocal Enforcement of Foreign Judgments Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: As the Family Justice Courts hear proceedings under these three Acts, these Acts will be amended to allow the Family Justice Rules Committee to make Family Justice Rules to prescribe the relevant procedure for proceedings under these Acts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will now turn to the amendments arising from the Mental Capacity Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Mental Capacity Act was passed in 2008, and it introduced two frameworks to deal with the issues arising from the lack of mental capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, it conferred powers for the Court to appoint deputies to make decisions on behalf of persons who lacked mental capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, it introduced the Lasting Power of Attorney, a legal instrument which allows individuals to appoint a "donee" to make decisions on their behalf should they lose mental capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill amends nine Acts to include the reference to a donee of a Lasting Power of Attorney under the Mental Capacity Act, where there is already a reference to a deputy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that donees will have the same standing as deputies under those Acts, when the donor loses mental capacity.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: I will next turn to the amendments which allow the designation of other political office holders to hear appeals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This is consistent with other newly introduced and recently amended laws and facilitates administration by allowing political officeholders to focus on various responsibilities and portfolios within the Ministry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: In 2015, Singapore signed a Joint Declaration with the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea (ITLOS) to allow ITLOS proceedings to be hosted in Singapore in future.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: ITLOS is an independent judicial body established by the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) to hear disputes concerning the interpretation or application of UNCLOS.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 12 of the Bill amends the International Organisations (Immunity and Privileges) Act to empower the Government to apply the Act to relevant international organisations and bring ITLOS within the scope of the Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This ensures that the Government has the power to grant the legal capacities and to confer the privileges and immunities necessary for ITLOS to carry out its functions in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 16 of the Bill also contains a number of amendments which were proposed by the Law Society of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First is allowing SILE to enact rules for the administration of the Part A Course and Examinations.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Since 2015, SILE has taken over the administration of Part A of the Bar Examinations, which is one of the requirements for overseas trained law graduates from overseas scheduled universities to become a qualified person.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The amendments to the Legal Profession Act will enable SILE to enact rules to administer and provide for the conditions for entry to the courses, tests and examinations for Part A.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Legal Profession Act and the Singapore Academy of Law Act will be amended to ensure that UniSIM Law School and the members of its faculty will have the same standing or restrictions as those which are correspondingly applicable to NUS, SMU or their faculty members.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, allowing the Presiding Judge of the Family Justice Courts and the Presiding Judge of the State Courts to refer matters to the Law Society or the Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Presently, any Judge, Judicial Commissioner, Senior Judge or International Judge of the Supreme Court may refer matters touching on the conduct of any regulated legal practitioner to the Law Society or the Disciplinary Tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: The Bill amends the Legal Profession Act to confer the same powers on the Presiding Judge of the Family Justice Courts and the Presiding Judge of the State Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Lastly, there are a number of amendments arising from requests made by the Law Society, which I will summarise.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: First, the composition of the Council of the Law Society will be amended in order to better reflect the composition of the members of the Law Society who are entitled to vote for the election of the members of the Council.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Second, it will no longer be compulsory for the voting of Council members to be conducted in a physical space via ballot.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Third, the Council will also be allowed to transfer certain amounts from the Compensation Fund to a fund established by the Law Society to purchase or maintain a library, where no grant is made from the Compensation Fund in any year and there is no application for a grant from the Compensation Fund that is pending at the end of that year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 15 amends the Legal Aid and Advice Act to enable the Legal Aid Bureau not to charge any registration fees for an application for legal aid or advice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This takes out one step in the registration process and makes it administratively more convenient for applicants when they apply for legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 35 amends the Remote Gambling Act 2014 to enlarge the jurisdiction of the District Court or a Magistrate's Court to try cases and sentence offenders under that Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: This allows the District Court or a Magistrate's Court to hear cases and impose the maximum fine or imprisonment term set out in the Remote Gambling Act 2014, notwithstanding the limits prescribed under the Criminal Procedure Code.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Currently, in contentious proceedings before the Registrar of Trade Marks, there is no avenue for appealing against interlocutory decisions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: There can be potentially severe consequences where interlocutory decisions have the effect of bringing proceedings to an end.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: An example would be when an interlocutory decision leads to a trademark application being treated as withdrawn.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah) (for the Minister for Law)
text: Clause 45 amends section 75 of the Trade Marks Act to allow for appeals in such situations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I declare that I am a lawyer with a Practising Certificate in force.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 50 of the Bill will introduce a new provision to the Wills Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This provision seems to be influenced by legislation in other countries, such as the United Kingdom (UK) Administration of Justice Act 1982, which contains a section 20 similar in wording to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have noted that an NUS law academic, Assoc Prof Barry Crown, had recommended that our Wills Act be amended to include such a statutory right to rectify a will to bring more certainty to this area of the law.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is because a 2014 case decided by the UK Supreme Court had suggested that the courts had a common law right to rectify wills even if there is no statutory right, and it is probably more prudent to legislate the right to make clear what powers the court should have.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Nevertheless, the UK case in question, Marley vs Rawlings, also raises questions about how wide the power under the new provision should be.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In that case, a husband and wife made mirror wills to leave their entire estate to a non-family member.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But each spouse signed the other spouse's will by mistake.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, the lawyer's office was at fault in not checking that the wills were executed by the proper party.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is way beyond the usual understanding of rectification being the adding or omitting of certain words only.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry intending the Court to have such a wide rectification power?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would also like a confirmation about the implication of such a provision on lawyers who have been negligent in drafting wills or in will execution.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will this provision save them from being liable for negligence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will clients be expected to go to Court first to try to rectify the will before suing lawyers for negligence?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would put a heavy burden on clients.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government Proceedings Act enables the Government to sue and to be sued.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 9 of the Bill amends section 29 of the Act to provide that, in such lawsuits, it is possible that the Court can certify that legal costs for more than two Government lawyers may be payable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is a change from the current position where the maximum number of Government lawyers a litigant may have to pay for is two.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to the explanatory note, the change is to bring the position in line with that in other civil suits and family matters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The current position in other civil suits and family matters is that the Court may order a litigant who loses to pay legal costs for more than two solicitors on the winning side.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In order for such a Court order to be obtained, the Court must find that more than two lawyers were reasonably required to handle the case due to factors, such as the complexity of the case or novel points of law being raised.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As it currently stands, anyone who is thinking of suing the Government or defending a legal action by the Government is aware that if the action is lost, he would likely have to pay legal costs to the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is on top of funding his own lawyers to meet the fierce challenges thrown by the Government's legal team, whose limitless resources include having the entire Legal Service and Civil Service at its disposal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not many individuals or entities have the financial resources needed to take the Government to Court or to defend a suit by the Government.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Government should consider taking a broader view on this matter and keep the current provision of capping its claim for legal costs to no more than two legal officers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: After all, the purpose of the Government Proceedings Act is to enable the Government to sue and to be sued.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the costs of suing or being sued by the Government are too high, people will surrender.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There must not be a signal sent that the Government is trying to use the prospect of crushing legal costs to deter or wear down those who may wish to sue the Government or to defend Government lawsuits vigorously.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clause 16 of the Bill makes various amendments to the Legal Profession Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My query relates to clauses 16(t) and (u) which deal with the disciplinary proceedings against lawyers who have misconducted themselves.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The act of giving gratifications for procuring legal services is generally abhorrent to the profession.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What sorts of exemptions are being contemplated and under what circumstances?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, I have two brief clarifications to be made.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Consequently, this removes the requirement for the Minister to lay that report before Parliament.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Based on my house visits and Meet-the-People Sessions, I sense an increasing number of neighbourly disputes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I value the work of the CMC, which provides a neutral platform for residents to resolve relational, social and community disputes amicably without resorting to litigation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Through community mediation, the CMC aims to cultivate a more harmonious, civil and gracious society.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also expect that the CMC will be facing an increasing amount of work.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I believe the report we are proposing to do away with, would be useful and crucial in allowing us to further detect issues in our community, detect trends, see what has worked and what has not and chart the way forward.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Senior Minister of State clarify why we are proposing this amendment and, if amended, will there be other forms of reports from the CMC and will these be made available to the public?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Currently, junior lawyers are practitioners with less than seven years of practice, middle category lawyers are those with between seven and 12 years of practice, and lawyers with more than 12 years of practice are senior lawyers.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Several amendments to the Act involve dealings by Government authorities with a person without mental capacity either through his Deputy or through his donee appointed under a Lasting Power of Attorney.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some of the amendments also allow the Minister to designate either the Second Minister, the Minister of State or Parliamentary Secretary to hear appeals.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I wish to raise two queries for the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Like my hon colleague Mr Louis Ng, I have a query about clause 3 of the Bill where section 21 of the Community Mediation Centres Act is repealed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: From an accountability point of view, when a Community Mediation Centre is established by the Government and funded by the Government, and the Director and staff are deemed public servants, surely the Director should continue to provide a report to the Minister.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This is to allow proper accountability of civil servants to the Executive arm of the Government.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am also of the view that the Minister ought to continue to lay the report before Parliament and account for the activities and efficacy of the Community Mediation Centres.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, could I ask the Senior Minister of State to clarify the rationale for repealing section 21 of the Community Mediation Centres Act?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The next clarification required is on the amendment to the Work Injury Compensation Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: His next-of-kin had purportedly accepted compensation under the Work Injury Compensation Act but, subsequently, his brother, who was appointed as a deputy under the Mental Capacity Act, then proceeded to sue the employer for damages under common law instead of claiming for compensation under the Work Injury Compensation Act.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: This section seems to suggest that the Commissioner of Labour continues to have the power to receive and pay compensation to any one or more of dependants even if there was no donee, even if there is no deputy appointed.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: A dependant under this Act is quite rightly crafted and it means the wife, husband, parent, grandparents, stepfather, stepmother, child, grandchild, stepchild, brother, sister, half-brother, half-sister, stepbrother, or stepsister, irrespective of whether that person is actually dependent on the employee's earnings or not.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If I may ask the Senior Minister of State, in light of the recent case in the High Court in April 2015, Justice Quentin Loh had made a decision and, in that decision, he had said that "In my judgement, the next-of-kin of a mentally incapacitated employee do not have, without more, the requisite capacity to make a claim under the Act on behalf of the employee.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Only a person duly appointed by the Court under the Mental Capacity Act will have the legal capacity to do so".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I am sorry if this House is struggling to understand what I am saying because this is quite legalistic.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: That was a High Court case made in April 2015 and, in March this year, the Court of Appeal had affirmed that particular decision.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In  light of what the Courts are saying, which is that only someone who is either a donee appointed under a Lasting Power of Attorney or someone who is appointed by the Court under the Mental Capacity Act as a deputy would have the power to make such a claim.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I think it would be useful for the Senior Minister of State to clarify that.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: With that, Mdm Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Louis Ng asked about the amendment to the Community Mediation Act and the removal of the need for the CMC to submit an Annual Report.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In this case, the CMC is a department of the Ministry of Law (MinLaw), which is held accountable through its accounts and budget estimates which are available in the annual Budget Book which is presented to Parliament.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: However, we do agree that information on the activities and the operations of the CMC should be available to the public.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Insofar, as information and statistics relating to the CMC are concerned, they will continue to be available on the CMC website, and this includes statistics on the number of mediations conducted, CMC's success rate and the types of disputes handled by CMC.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in other words, wherever you see deputy, the donee will have the same standing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: This particular amendment is not intended to address the larger question, which is whether other third parties are entitled to file claims or receive compensation under WICA.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There has been a recent decision by the Court of Appeal, as Mr Lim Biow Chuan has alluded to, on this wider issue, and the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) is studying the implications of this decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it would be premature for me to make any remarks on that at this moment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: MOM would see what implication the Court of Appeal's decision has.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With regard to the amendments to the Legal Profession Act, Mr Louis Ng queried the possible underlying causes leading to the shrinking middle category of lawyers and what steps were being taken to address this concern.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In May 2013, the report of the 4th Committee on the Supply of Lawyers identified three main factors as causing or contributing to attrition among legal professionals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: They were unsustainable work practices, unsuitability of the individual legal professional for legal work and structural problems within law firms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: To address this issue of attrition, the 4th Committee recommended that the two existing local law schools should consider a more targeted selection of law school applicants and help prepare young graduates early for the realities of practice, for example, by expanding clinical legal programmes currently offered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And to address the work-life balance concerns by providing flexibility in legal practice, for example, allowing flexible schedules or different career tracks for lawyers and by providing greater support and welfare, for example, by providing lawyers with tools to create a better working environment.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Tackling these issues will take time and require a concerted effort on the part of the law schools and the legal profession as a whole.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Steps are being taken to look into this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Law Society is presently conducting a study to look into how junior lawyers can be encouraged to stay in practice which, in turn, will help the number of lawyers in this middle category.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The findings of their study should be available later in the year.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also longer-term initiatives which have taken these concerns into account.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For example, the third law school at UniSIM will select its students based not just on academic ability but also aptitude, attitude and interest in the practice of family and criminal law.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Their curriculum will be practice-oriented, culminating in a six-month practicum training, so that students will be better prepared and equipped for the realities of practice.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, this will deal, to some extent, with the second problem identified by the 4th Committee, in relation to the unsuitability of individuals for legal work.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I should also highlight that the lawyers represented by the original middle category are more limited, compared to the junior and senior categories.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It represents five cohorts of lawyers: those between seven and 12 years of standing.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In comparison, the junior and senior categories represent lawyers under seven years' standing and not less than 12 years' standing respectively, which is a larger number of cohorts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In addition, the statistics relate to the number of lawyers who remain in private practice in law firms.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Some of those who leave private practice remain in the legal profession as in-house counsel in the private sector, or by joining the public sector or academia.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Others move into other industries, such as investment banking, fund management, private equity, where their legal skills come in useful, and they continue to make a meaningful contribution to the wider economy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I believe Ms Sylvia Lim has asked a number of questions, the first relating to the Wills Act and the scope of the power to be given to the Courts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: First, she did not touch on my query on the Legal Profession Act amendments, clause 16(t) and (u).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: What are the circumstances contemplated under which the Minister would prescribe rules to exempt lawyers who had, on the face of it, committed some misconduct, according to what is raised in the Bill?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that it was spurred on by the recent Court of Appeal's case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: But I would like her to confirm whether the inspiration for the wording came from the UK and whether she is aware of the case which I cited, Marley vs Rawlings, which interpreted that provision very widely and whether it is the intention of the Government to give the Court this kind of width of rectification power.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: My third clarification concerns the cost of Government proceedings.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that this does not give the Government additional powers, but the fact is that under the existing section 29 of the Government Proceedings Act (GPA), the cost claimable is limited to two.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, this amendment would actually give an allowance for the Court to certify more than two lawyers' costs being payable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: It is a change to the legal position, as far as  GPA is concerned.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the safeguard there is that it lies in the hands of the Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the question on the Wills Act, I am not able to comment if there was a specific reference to the UK case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That, really, is, as I have stated, the intent behind this.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the third question, I think that the Minister would have to look at it on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am not setting out any specific guidelines in this instance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But basically, when the Minister looks at it, he would have due regard as to what cases should be exempted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The point here, of course, is that when you have the Government on one side of a legal proceeding and perhaps a private individual or private entity on the other side, you are dealing with an inequality of resources in most cases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: The Government, with its Legal Officers, having the whole Civil Service there, the prospect of a litigant going into litigation with the Government and sustaining that litigation, I think it is already prohibitive to most people.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, my question is, why is the Government not able to take a broader view, you may want to say, even a magnanimous view or perhaps a view from the accountability standpoint that, look, we are not going to allow cost to be an inhibition or prohibitive factor when the litigant decides whether to continue with litigation or to commence litigation with the Government or not.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I am sure the Government does not need the money.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: So, the question is, why do you need to change that position to allow for more than two lawyers' costs to be claimed?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Why can the Government not limit its position to two?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I just want to flag that as a first point.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there are any number of parties with different situations and they may have different financial means.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The second point as to why it is necessary or why should the Government not limit itself, the answer is that there is no one size fits all when it comes to the issue of costs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There will be some instances where a lot of work is required and where it is very complex, and where there will be others where it is much more straightforward and simpler.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: At the end of the day, it is really for the Court to decide.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And our Courts, in this matter, I believe, are objective and fair.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, at the end of the day, I think it rests with the Court to do the right thing, with respect to costs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Regarding the case law of the UK case that is cited by Ms Sylvia Lim, I just want to ask for the Senior Minister of State's clarification.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am not sure I understand the Senior Minister of State's answer, but I think for judicial guidance, if it is not the intention of the Government that the UK Supreme Court decision is intended to be applied, then perhaps the Government can state its position now so that the Courts will be able to follow accordingly when the Bill is passed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I am sorry if I was not sufficiently clear just now.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, it was prompted by our Court of Appeal's decision, but when the Government drafted these provisions, the Government did look at the UK case and some of the wordings were based on that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is as far as I can go.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Obviously, when our Courts apply it, and when they look at other precedents, our Courts will have to give effect to the law as our Courts see correct.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What I do not want to do, is to suggest in any way that our Courts are bound by another court's decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the short answer to the Member's question of whether we looked at the UK case in question, the answer is yes.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But as to what was it that prompted this particular amendment, it was our Court of Appeal's decision.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it would not be our approach to use costs to be oppressive, but to seek costs where we think that it is fairly and justly incurred and to leave it to the Court to make the appropriate decision on the quantum of costs to be awarded and the number of counsels to be taken into account.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: So, you have no choice whether you think you are being wrongly or rightly prosecuted, but because you look at the cost, you say, "Oh let's forget about it, let's pay." So, is that a good thing for Singapore as a society?

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: That the people who feel somehow victimised by the Government are intimidated by the cost; you do not know how much the Court is going to decide.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the past, you said, "Okay, it is limited to two lawyers", but now, there will be more.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As I have indicated, when the Government has to defend a matter or pursue a matter, it will do so after having taken advice, doing so rationally and doing so if it thinks that it is the right course of action.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That is the first thing when it comes to taking proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With respect to the amount of costs that a person may face, when a person brings proceedings against the Government, that person would, no doubt, be legally advised, and also have an indication of the amount of costs that would be incurred.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And it should not be forgotten that if costs ought to be awarded against that party, it does mean that that party, at the end of the day, ultimately failed against the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Meaning that, that case should not have been brought in the first place.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And the final safeguard is really the Court.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is in the hands of the Court to ensure that the amounts of costs that are awarded are fair and just.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And as I have said, this Government will pursue a course that is reasonable and rational and that the costs sought are commensurate with the claim.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is not the intention of the Government to intimidate anyone.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Mr Low, I must stop this clarification, because you have made your point, Ms Sylvia Lim has made the same point, Mr Dennis Tan has made the same point, clarification sought.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Indranee Rajah has already made her replies.

speaker: Mdm Speaker
text: I do not think there is going to be any further development by continuing with the clarification.      .
